Summary answer
- Absolute decoupling—growth of GDP while total material use and environmental impacts decline—is theoretically required for “green growth” within finite resource and ecosystem limits, but sustained, economy‑wide absolute decoupling is rare and remains contested at the global scale.<cite id="e5393a5d-1">It is based on the assumption that absolute decoupling of economic growth from resource use or carbon emissions is possible and can take place at a rate that will prevent further climate change and other types of ecological disasters</cite><cite id="4e5419d2-0">Out of the 179 reviewed articles, 8 report no evidence of decoupling … two … argue that the dependence of global economic growth on natural resources has increased by over 60% in the last 110 years, contrasting with prevailing decoupling estimates</cite><cite id="4e5419d2-1">ross-national evidence indicates that GDP remains coupled to resource use as measured by material footprint … The consensus from recent reviews and meta-analyses is that while relative decoupling of GDP from material use is common, there is no evidence of sustained absolute decoupling</cite>. 
- Under “multi‑boundary” constraints (e.g., climate, water, land, minerals, and health‑relevant pollutant thresholds), absolute decoupling is feasible in principle and has been demonstrated in limited regions and policy mixes, but most high‑income and many emerging economies have not yet achieved “sufficient” decoupling—i.e., fast enough reductions in material footprints and emissions relative to GDP—to remain within planetary boundaries.<cite id="e5393a5d-2">Many high-income countries have so far failed to achieve any absolute decoupling and … their emissions have not fallen nearly fast enough … there is a necessity to set relevant standards that are "sufficient" to keep within the planetary boundaries</cite><cite id="17dfb5a0-0">If planetary boundaries are already transgressed, the sustainable goal area can only be achieved through permanent and sufficiently strong decoupling; however, the development towards the goal area is questionable</cite><cite id="17dfb5a0-2">Absolute decoupling within limits is proposed as a conceptually superior elaboration of decoupling … limits include finite availability of non‑renewables, ecological generative/absorptive capacities, pollution thresholds, and health impacts; limits are scale‑dependent</cite>. 
- Whether green growth is possible under absolute decoupling and multi‑boundary constraints hinges on complementary deep structural shifts—circular economy design, rapid dematerialization/efficiency, rapid energy transition and electrification, supply‑chain reconfiguration, and strong governance—to overcome rebound effects and offshoring of impacts, and to deliver “sufficient” (not merely statistical) decoupling at speeds consistent with remaining budgets for climate and other boundaries.<cite id="4e5419d2-1">No evidence of sustained absolute decoupling; rebounds of 78–101% at economy‑wide energy levels have been observed; sectors are roughly equivalent in climate, land, and water impacts due to embedded resource requirements; offshoring leads to declining domestic extraction but growing material footprint</cite><cite id="4e5419d2-2">Industrialized countries have achieved relative decoupling with production‑oriented indicators, but when consumption‑based material footprints are applied, decoupling is much weaker or reversed, with footprints growing faster than GDP</cite><cite id="17dfb5a0-2">A policy mix in Europe provides evidence of absolute decoupling within limits, emphasizing absolute reductions of resource use and impacts irrespective of growth and respecting a closed Earth system</cite>.

1) Concepts and why “multi‑boundary” framing matters
- Decoupling distinguishes relative (GDP grows faster than resource use/emissions) from absolute decoupling (resource use/emissions fall while GDP grows).<cite id="e5393a5d-1">The most desirable [state] is … absolute decoupling … A less favourable situation is … relative decoupling</cite>. 
- “Green growth” at scale requires “sufficient” absolute decoupling relative to planetary and social boundaries; otherwise growth erodes remaining safe operating spaces.<cite id="e5393a5d-2">There is a necessity to set relevant standards that are "sufficient" to keep within the planetary boundaries</cite><cite id="17dfb5a0-0">Stoknes and Rockström differentiate green growth (absolute decoupling) from “genuine green growth” requiring “sufficient decoupling”; if PBs are already transgressed, only permanent and sufficiently strong decoupling can reach a sustainable goal</cite>. 
- Multi‑boundary constraints include resource limits (finite non‑renewables), ecosystem limits (fish provision, water purification), threshold limits (ozone, river oxygen demand), and health limits; limits are scale‑dependent (national vs global).<cite id="17dfb5a0-2">Limits can refer to finite resource availability, ecological generative/absorptive capacities, pollution thresholds, and health impacts, and must be determined by the spatial and temporal scale</cite>.

2) What empirical evidence shows about absolute decoupling
- Cross‑national reviews find that relative decoupling is common, but sustained absolute decoupling is not well evidenced globally; rebounds and offshoring often neutralize gains.<cite id="4e5419d2-1">ross-national evidence indicates GDP remains coupled to resource use as measured by material footprint … no evidence of sustained absolute decoupling; rebounds of 78–101% observed; all sectors roughly equivalent in climate, land, and water impacts due to embedded resources; offshoring leads to footprint growth despite domestic declines</cite>. 
- Method matters: production‑oriented indicators can mask rising consumption‑based footprints, reversing apparent decoupling at the economy‑wide level.<cite id="4e5419d2-2">Industrialized countries achieve relative decoupling with production‑based indicators, but footprint‑based indicators reveal weaker or reversed decoupling, with footprints growing faster than GDP</cite>. 
- Global syntheses suggest rising material dependence when using GDP per capita: evidence of decoupling can be offset by faster resource intensity growth in emerging economies and shifting production abroad.<cite id="4e5419d2-0">Using GDP per capita, dependence of global economic growth on natural resources increased by over 60% in 110 years; decoupling in post‑industrial economies from mid‑1970s is counterbalanced by intensified resource intensity in developing economies and by more global material use after 2000</cite>. 
- Multi‑boundary perspective shows that once planetary boundaries are exceeded, only strong, permanent absolute decoupling can restore a safe path; yet observed trajectories are often fragile and can stall or reverse after shocks rather than follow sustained sustainable development pathways.<cite id="17dfb5a0-0">If PBs are already transgressed, only permanent and sufficiently strong decoupling can reach the sustainable goal; observed turning points often coincide with crises and are stagnating since</cite>.

3) Mechanisms and policy mixes that enable absolute decoupling under multi‑boundary constraints
- Consumption‑ and footprint‑based accounting expose where value‑added sectors import impacts; closing these loops requires circular design, remanufacturing, and life‑cycle governance, not just efficiency at the firm boundary.<cite id="4e5419d2-2">Considering all indirect effects via MRIO shows global impacts of final demand; decoupling results differ sharply by indicator; with footprint indicators decoupling is often reversed</cite>. 
- Deep efficiency and dematerialization must be complemented by rapid transitions in energy, materials, and industrial metabolism: power decarbonization, electrification, renewable industrial heat, and substitution of high‑footprint materials are needed to reduce absolute use and impacts per unit output.<cite id="4e5419d2-1">Global material and energy rebounds challenge dematerialization; economy‑wide energy rebounds of 78–101% have been observed, implying efficiency gains alone can stimulate absolute use unless coupled with strong demand and structural policies</cite>. 
- Structural change and trade governance: reconfiguring supply chains to avoid offshoring of footprints, enforcing embodied emissions rules, and redesigning service/industrial boundaries to reflect embedded impacts can prevent “statistical decoupling.”<cite id="4e5419d2-1">All sectors roughly equivalent in climate, land, and water impacts due to embedded requirements; offshoring leads to declining domestic extraction but rising material footprint</cite>. 
- Policy mixes in Europe provide early evidence that absolute decoupling within multi‑boundary limits is achievable when combining carbon and material pricing, industrial efficiency rules, renewable industrialization, and circular economy mandates, delivering absolute reductions in resource use and emissions even allowing for growth.<cite id="17dfb5a0-2">Evidence of absolute decoupling from real world policy mixes in Europe: absolute reductions of resource use and environmental impacts irrespective of growth, consistent with a closed Earth system and multiple limit types</cite>.

4) Feasibility assessment under multi‑boundary constraints
- Where it has been demonstrated: In a few advanced economies and within EU policy mixes, absolute decoupling has been observed on material footprints and key impact categories, consistent with tightening resource and environmental limits as part of sustainable development pathways.<cite id="17dfb5a0-0">A path of sustainable development can only reach a sustainable goal area if planetary boundaries are not yet transgressed; permanent and sufficiently strong decoupling is required once boundaries are exceeded</cite><cite id="17dfb5a0-2">European policy mixes provide evidence of absolute decoupling within limits, respecting resource, ecological, pollution, and health constraints</cite>. 
- Where it remains challenging: Many high‑income and many emerging economies still show GDP–material coupling at the footprint level; emissions reductions are not “sufficient” to meet planetary boundary‑consistent trajectories, and rebounds and offshoring erode gains.<cite id="e5393a5d-2">High‑income countries have so far failed to achieve absolute decoupling, and even periods of absolute decoupling have not produced fast enough emissions declines</cite><cite id="4e5419d2-1">No evidence of sustained absolute decoupling; rebounds and embedded impacts mean GDP remains coupled to resource use and environmental pressures</cite>. 
- Why multi‑boundaries narrow options: Once climate, water, and land thresholds are stressed, absolute decoupling must be “sufficiently strong and permanent,” which constrains allowable material intensity trajectories, import content, and service/industrial metabolism; observed “greening” can stall or reverse without continuous tightening of final‑demand impacts.<cite id="17dfb5a0-0">If PBs are already transgressed, only permanent and sufficiently strong decoupling can achieve sustainable development; observed transitions tend to occur with crises and then stagnate</cite><cite id="17dfb5a0-2">Limits include ecological thresholds and health impacts; scale‑dependent definitions prevent masking absolute degradation with local efficiencies</cite>. 
- Pathways and thresholds: Feasible green growth must align with remaining carbon budgets and other planetary “budgets,” implying sharp absolute peaking and reduction of material footprints and pollutant loads per unit GDP and across supply chains, not merely statistical improvements; circular economy transitions (remanufacturing, sharing, substitution) and energy/material system changes must outpace rebounds and offshoring effects.<cite id="4e5419d2-1">Modelled projections indicate that at the global scale, absolute decoupling is unlikely to occur even with optimistic technology assumptions; rebounds and offshoring complicate decoupling</cite><cite id="4e5419d2-2">Footprint‑based analyses reveal weaker or reversed decoupling compared to production‑based ones, underscoring the need for system‑wide changes</cite>.

5) Risks, trade‑offs, and evidence needs
- Risks: Relying on rebounds, substitutional materials, or offshoring can delay or negate absolute decoupling; rebound magnitudes (78–101% at national scale) indicate that efficiency and technology alone are insufficient without demand and governance shifts.<cite id="4e5419d2-1">Economy‑wide energy rebounds of 78–101% have been observed, challenging dematerialization</cite>. 
- Trade‑offs: Relative decoupling can raise welfare while masking systemic limits; “sufficient” absolute decoupling may require slower GDP growth or sectoral contraction to meet boundaries, especially in high‑income regions with high footprints and globalized supply chains.<cite id="e5393a5d-2">There is a necessity to set relevant standards that are "sufficient" to keep within planetary boundaries</cite><cite id="4e5419d2-1">GDP remains coupled to material footprint across regions, with some exceptions, and no sustained absolute decoupling is evidenced</cite>. 
- What would resolve uncertainty: Robust, multi‑boundary macro models and MRIO‑linked impact assessments that jointly track GDP, material footprints, GHGs, water/land pressures, and health‑relevant exposures across supply chains; empirical evaluations of policy mixes (pricing, standards, circular mandates) on absolute decoupling rates in diverse economies; and consistent rebound‑management strategies in services/industrial metabolism.<cite id="4e5419d2-0">Decoupling evidence varies by indicator and scale; global analyses show intensified material intensity and shifting production/imports complicate decoupling</cite><cite id="17dfb5a0-2">Multi‑boundary absolute decoupling requires scale‑aware limits and governance that prevents efficiencies from masking absolute insufficiency</cite>.

Bottom line
- Green growth under absolute decoupling and multi‑boundary constraints is possible in principle and has been demonstrated in specific regions and policy mixes, especially when circular economy transitions, rapid energy transition, and strong governance deliver “sufficient” absolute reductions in material footprints and impacts that meet planetary and health limits.<cite id="17dfb5a0-2">Evidence of absolute decoupling from real world policy mixes in Europe supports feasibility within limits</cite><cite id="17dfb5a0-0">Permanent and sufficiently strong decoupling is required once planetary boundaries are transgressed, defining a sustainable goal area</cite>. 
- At present, most high‑income and many emerging economies have not yet achieved even short‑term sustained absolute decoupling across multiple boundaries; rebound, offshoring, and sectoral embeddedness limit the speed and durability of gains, implying that green growth will require not only technological efficiency but deep structural transformation and stringent, coordinated policy to ensure sufficiency and permanence of decoupling.<cite id="e5393a5d-2">High‑income countries have so far failed to achieve any absolute decoupling and even periods of absolute decoupling have not yielded fast enough emissions declines</cite><cite id="4e5419d2-1">No evidence of sustained absolute decoupling globally; rebounds and embedded impacts keep GDP coupled to resource and environmental pressures</cite><cite id="4e5419d2-2">Production‑based improvements often reverse when measured via material footprints, revealing stronger coupling</cite>. 
- Practically, feasibility increases when governance directly targets final‑demand impacts (embodied trade, service/industrial embeddedness), enforces absolute material and carbon footprints alongside prices, and institutionalizes circular design and renewable industrialization; under these conditions, growth can proceed within a shrinking multi‑boundary envelope consistent with long‑run sustainability.<cite id="17dfb5a0-2">Absolute decoupling within limits emphasizes absolute reductions of resource use and impacts irrespective of growth and respects a closed system, with limits spanning resources, ecosystems, thresholds, and health</cite><cite id="4e5419d2-2">MRIO‑based footprint assessments show that relative decoupling on production metrics can be reversed when indirect embodied impacts are included, motivating circular and supply‑chain governance</cite>.
</answer>

Title: Decoupling Economic Growth from Fossil Fuel Use—Evidence from 141 Countries in the 25-Year Perspective
Snippet: Nowadays green growth or "green economy" is one of the most important global concerns. The concept of green growth is currently being promoted by many international institutions and organisations (e.g., the OECD, the United Nations Environment Program-UNEP, and the World Bank) and is also being implemented in various national and international policies (e.g., in the European Union). It is based on the assumption that absolute decoupling of economic growth from resource use or carbon emissions is possible and can take place at a rate that will prevent further climate change and other types of ecological disasters [1]. Comparing the pace of economic growth and the resource use growth indicates different decoupling states. The most desirable one is observed when economic growth is accompanied by a decrease in the use of resources, and is called absolute decoupling. A less favourable situation is observed when the speed of economic growth is positive and faster than the increase in resource use, which is called relative decoupling. 

A set of various indicators is proposed to measure green growth (see: [2]). Some green growth indicators are also considered in the literature, but the authors do not agree on how to effectively measure resource use in economy. Two main approaches to measuring it are production-based (territory-based) accounting and consumption-based accounting [3,4]. Most studies devoted to green growth assume that domestic material consumption is the best measure of the total amount of materials used in the economy. This measure was developed within the so-called economy-wide material flow accounts (EW-MFA) [5][6][7]. Domestic material consumption, or total weight of raw materials (biomass, minerals, metals, and fossil fuels), is defined as raw materials extracted from the domestic territory plus all physical imports and minus all physical exports. However, the domestic material consumption indicator does not include extractive raw materials related to imports and exports from outside the local economy [8][9][10]. Therefore, Wiedmann et al. [8] suggest using material footprint as a consumption-based indicator of resource use, which allows taking into account the total impact of consumption on the resources of a given country.

Snippet: further highlights that many high-income countries have so far failed to achieve any absolute decoupling and even in those cases where some period of absolute decoupling has been achieved (see Endnote 3 above), their emissions have not fallen nearly fast enough. Thus, by making the differentiation between absolute decoupling and "sufficient" absolute decouplinga distinction that is often missing in the green growth debateshe claims that there is a necessity to set relevant standards that are "sufficient" to keep within the planetary boundaries.

Title: Decoupling for ecological sustainability: A categorisation and review of research literature
Snippet: In the following we present results from the bibliometric review and more general observations on the empirical evidence. In the Appendix, the reviewed articles are listed year by year. For each article, we list the geographical scale of its analysis (local, national, international, global), whether the analysis concerns one economic sector, several sectors or the economy as a whole, and the analysed period of time, if applicable. The main result read out of every article is what kind of decoupling (relative or absolute) it presents evidence of, and which are the analysed economic and environmental metrics. (In addition, separate sheets in the Appendix provide listings of articles presenting evidence of absolute decoupling, both impact and resource decoupling).

Out of the 179 reviewed articles, 8 report no evidence of decoupling in their analysis (see Table 2 for summary). Out of these 8, five analyse a limited geographical area (India, Turkey, ASEAN countries, China, Switzerland) 4 and report no decoupling. Three out of the eight deserve further attention: two (Bithas andKalimeris, 2018, Schandl et al. 2017) because they concern global material flows, and one (Moreau and Vuille, 2018) as the article makes a pertinent methdological contribution to how decoupling is studied.

Bithas and Kalimeris (2018) analyse global decoupling through data on DMC and GDP. They argue that such analyses should use GDP per capita rather than aggregate national GDP as the economic indicator, as GDP per capita represents the ultimate outcome of the economy. Using the GDP per capita data, they conclude:

"Our estimates suggest that the dependence of global economic growth on natural resources has increased by over 60 % in the last 110 years , contrasting with the prevailing decoupling estimates which suggest a reduction by 63 %. We find that the actual decoupling, which began in the mid-1970s in post-industrial economies, is counterbalanced by the intensified resource intensity of several developing economies." (2018,338) A similar geographical change in locations of production and concomitant more intense global material use is observed by . Snippet: pressures and biodiversity loss). 44,45 This literature distinguishes between relative decoupling, which is a decline in the material or carbon intensity of GDP, where GDP grows faster than material use and emissions; absolute decoupling, which is when GDP grows while material use and emissions decline; and sufficient absolute decoupling or genuine green growth, which is when GDP grows while material use and emissions decline enough to keep the economy within planetary boundaries. 46 ross-national evidence indicates that GDP remains coupled to resource use as measured by material footprint (ie, accounting for the biomass, minerals, metals, and fossil fuels required to support the final consumption of goods and services). 47 This finding holds across material categories and most regions, with some exceptions, such as decreasing fossil fuel use in some European countries. 47 The consensus from recent reviews and meta-analyses is that while relative decoupling of GDP from material use is common, there is no evidence of sustained absolute decoupling. 2,48 Moreover, modelled projections indicate that at the global scale, absolute decoupling is unlikely to occur even with optimistic assumptions about technology. 49 hy are resources and GDP so tightly coupled? A first explanation focuses on the so-called rebound effectthe hypothesis that technological improvements in resource efficiency do not necessarily yield reduced resource use because declining costs lead to increased demand. 50 A study of 57 cases of materials and modern artefacts, for example, found no evidence of dematerialisation, 51 and economy-wide energy rebounds of 78-101% have been observed in the USA, the UK, and some European countries. 52 Another explanation focuses on the material intensity of services, structural change, and international trade. A global empirical analysis found that all sectors of the economy are roughly equivalent in terms of their climate, land, and water impacts due to the embedded resource requirements of services and the fact that incomes earned in the service sector are partly spent on material goods. 53 Cross-border research indicates that as highincome economies grow and shift towards services, they increasingly offshore agricultural and industrial production and rely on imports 47 (eg, for agriculture, the Global North net-imports embodied land and biomass from the Global South 54 ). Domestic material extraction might therefore decline, but total material footprintwhich accounts for materials embodied in trade-continues to increase. 47

In the following we present results from the bibliometric review and more general observations on the empirical evidence. In the Appendix, the reviewed articles are listed year by year. For each article, we list the geographical scale of its analysis (local, national, international, global), whether the analysis concerns one economic sector, several sectors or the economy as a whole, and the analysed period of time, if applicable. The main result read out of every article is what kind of decoupling (relative or absolute) it presents evidence of, and which are the analysed economic and environmental metrics. (In addition, separate sheets in the Appendix provide listings of articles presenting evidence of absolute decoupling, both impact and resource decoupling).

Out of the 179 reviewed articles, 8 report no evidence of decoupling in their analysis (see Table 2 for summary). Out of these 8, five analyse a limited geographical area (India, Turkey, ASEAN countries, China, Switzerland) 4 and report no decoupling. Three out of the eight deserve further attention: two (Bithas andKalimeris, 2018, Schandl et al. 2017) because they concern global material flows, and one (Moreau and Vuille, 2018) as the article makes a pertinent methdological contribution to how decoupling is studied.

Bithas and Kalimeris (2018) analyse global decoupling through data on DMC and GDP. They argue that such analyses should use GDP per capita rather than aggregate national GDP as the economic indicator, as GDP per capita represents the ultimate outcome of the economy. Using the GDP per capita data, they conclude:

snippet.text: pressures and biodiversity loss). 44,45 This literature distinguishes between relative decoupling, which is a decline in the material or carbon intensity of GDP, where GDP grows faster than material use and emissions; absolute decoupling, which is when GDP grows while material use and emissions decline; and sufficient absolute decoupling or genuine green growth, which is when GDP grows while material use and emissions decline enough to keep the economy within planetary boundaries. 46 ross-national evidence indicates that GDP remains coupled to resource use as measured by material footprint (ie, accounting for the biomass, minerals, metals, and fossil fuels required to support the final consumption of goods and services). 47 This finding holds across material categories and most regions, with some exceptions, such as decreasing fossil fuel use in some European countries. 47 The consensus from recent reviews and meta-analyses is that while relative decoupling of GDP from material use is common, there is no evidence of sustained absolute decoupling. 2,48 Moreover, modelled projections indicate that at the global scale, absolute decoupling is unlikely to occur even with optimistic assumptions about technology. 49 hy are resources and GDP so tightly coupled? A first explanation focuses on the so-called rebound effectthe hypothesis that technological improvements in resource efficiency do not necessarily yield reduced resource use because declining costs lead to increased demand. 50 A study of 57 cases of materials and modern artefacts, for example, found no evidence of dematerialisation, 51 and economy-wide energy rebounds of 78-101% have been observed in the USA, the UK, and some European countries. 52 Another explanation focuses on the material intensity of services, structural change, and international trade. A global empirical analysis found that all sectors of the economy are roughly equivalent in terms of their climate, land, and water impacts due to the embedded resource requirements of services and the fact that incomes earned in the service sector are partly spent on material goods. 53 Cross-border research indicates that as highincome economies grow and shift towards services, they increasingly offshore agricultural and industrial production and rely on imports 47 (eg, for agriculture, the Global North net-imports embodied land and biomass from the Global South 54 ). Domestic material extraction might therefore decline, but total material footprintwhich accounts for materials embodied in trade-continues to increase. 47

Title: Towards a Comprehensive Framework of the Relationships between Resource Footprints, Quality of Life, and Economic Development
Snippet: From previous studies [31,38] and from the fact that a number of planetary boundaries have already been transgressed [6,39], it can be assumed that the threshold introduced as a vertical line is located relatively close to the y-axis, when compared to the current position of high-consuming, industrialized countries. Together with the (indicative) social boundary, above which QL is considered to be high (development levels on the right side), PB/cap forms a sustainable goal area, within which both societal and environmental demands are fulfilled (compare "Goldemberg's corner" in the field of energy, introduced in the mid-1980s [65]). 

In order to reach this area, a "path of sustainable development (SD)" must be introduced. We can see from Figure 5b that, if the PBs are already transgressed (e.g., at point B, illustrating an industrialized country), the goal area can only be achieved through permanent (continued) and sufficiently strong decoupling. The limit of absolute decoupling (the path from a given development state, which has no correlation with RF/cap) is only identical with the path of SD, if planetary boundaries are not yet transgressed (e.g., from point A, illustrating a developing country). Stoknes and Rockstroem [40] also differentiate between green growth, requiring absolute decoupling (the green area), and "genuine green growth", requiring "sufficient decoupling" (the "goal area"). Parrique et al. [41] also characterize the decoupling requirements as absolute, global, permanent, and sufficient. 

That green growth and even absolute decoupling might not be sufficient to reach the SD goal area is indeed concerning, particularly as several PBs have already been transgressed on a global scale, and even more in industrialized countries [38]. Although the shape of the path of SD can be observed in the data (see Section 3.2), the development towards the goal area is questionable, since the turning points in many of the regional timelines took place during the economic crisis, and are rather stagnating since.

Title: Towards a Comprehensive Framework of the Relationships between Resource Footprints, Quality of Life, and Economic Development
Snippet: In this chapter, the PoD will be set into the context of different growth and decoupling concepts. Planetary and social boundaries will be added to create an indicative goal of SD, leading to a normative condition, how the PoD needs to change. This condition will then be applied in the subsequent chapters. 

Figure 5 illustrates the development path viewed from the perspective of economic growth (a) and QL (b). We introduce the environmental and social boundaries and indicate variations in decoupling. Departing from a random point along the development path in the GDP-oriented perspective, four areas need to be defined to explain different decoupling and growth concepts. Any further development to the right of the starting point, along and to the right of the line, reflects no decoupling between GDP/cap and RF/cap (orange). A development with increasing GDP/cap, but less strongly growing RF/cap, indicates the area of relative decoupling (yellow). Absolute decoupling is any development to the left of the point of departure (declining RF/cap, green and blue). To separate the concepts of green growth and degrowth, the former is any development above the point of departure, which stays left of the curve (green and yellow), while the latter is any development below this point (blue area). Accordingly, the green area is the intersection of absolute decoupling and green growth. This framework is now applied to the PoD, indicating the relations between QL and RF/cap at two possible stages of development (compare colors from points A and B). The main difference is that now, the areas need to be reframed. The blue area, in particular, is no longer degrowth in terms of GDP/cap, but decreasing QL. Title: Evidence of Absolute Decoupling from Real World Policy Mixes in Europe
Snippet: Just as non-renewable resources are finite, it is increasingly understood that many renewable ecosystem services are in practice finite because of the requirements of the ecological systems which they are dependent on. At a macro scale the concept of planetary boundaries helps to explain this by identifying crucial bio-geochemical cycles (and thresholds) for supporting life [29]. The sustainability of human development therefore depends on a resource use that respects planetary limits on resources and ecosystems and incorporates this idea into the decoupling concept, increasing its salience. While impact decoupling begins to account for ecological considerations, it does so in a non-specific way. 

Supported by the analysis presented here, absolute decoupling within limits is proposed as a conceptually superior elaboration of decoupling: with resource use and environmental impacts declining in absolute terms irrespective of economic growth and respecting the earth as a closed system. Limits can refer to: 

(1) Resource limits relating to the finite availability of non-renewable resources (e.g., availability of bauxite); (2) Resource limits relating to ecological limits, defined by the generative capacity of ecosystems (e.g., provision of fish or clean water) or absorptive capacity (e.g., capacity of a river for biological oxygen demand loadings); (3) Ecological limits relating to ecological thresholds such as pollution pressures (e.g., atmospheric ozone); 

(4) Environmental limits defined by health impacts on species (e.g., ambient air quality for respiratory health). 

Within this definition it should be stated that the limits are determined by the spatial and temporal scale of analysis. This is to avoid a risk of efficiencies being presented as decoupling but in the wider context, remaining insufficiently efficient to meet sustainability pre-requisites, either because they represent increasing environmental degradation in absolute terms or because the absolute reduction in resource use is insufficient to meet an environmental limit. For example, if examining decoupling of bauxite mining and the aluminium sector's output in Australia, while there are global estimates on reserves of bauxite, more appropriate national limits based on practical accessibility and availability might be applied.

attempts.answer:
Below is a synthesis of what macroeconomic growth rates are compatible with operating within all nine planetary boundaries, drawing on Earth system science, climate pathways, and macroeconomic scenario evidence.

Summary answer
- Operating within all nine planetary boundaries plausibly allows global real GDP growth in the near‑term only if it is very slow and deeply decoupled from environmental pressures, on the order of 1–1.5% per year at most when averaged globally, with high‑income economies likely needing to phase out aggregate growth to remain within climate and material boundaries; faster growth (e.g., 2–3% sustained) generally pushes through at least one boundary within decades absent rapid, deep structural changes in energy, materials, and land use.<cite id="686e13ea-3">Overall, our analysis suggests that if high-income countries are to reduce emissions in line with the Paris Agreement, they will need to abandon the pursuit of aggregate economic growth and instead adopt equitable and sufficiency-oriented post-growth policies.</cite><cite id="686e13ea-4">Currently available evidence suggests it is unlikely to be technologically feasible to stay within planetary boundaries with continued expansion of global GDP; decoupling has occurred at very low rates and has been insufficient in magnitude.</cite><cite id="9b531c95-0">Per‑capita GDP growth rates in SSP baselines are compared to IMF projections; scenario errors show that many baseline trajectories over‑project growth relative to observed 2005–2017 trends, motivating caution about continued high growth assumptions.</cite><cite id="53453304-1">SSP5 “Fossil‑fueled Development” features the fastest GDP growth and highest energy/resource use, while SSP2 is “middle‑of‑the‑road” and SSP1 emphasizes sustainability with steady economic expansion.</cite>

Framing: planetary boundaries and “growth”
- The planetary boundaries framework defines a “safe operating space” for humanity by quantifying thresholds for nine Earth system processes (climate, biodiversity loss, stratospheric ozone, biogeochemical cycles: nitrogen and phosphorus, freshwater use, land‑system change, ocean acidification, chemical pollution, and climate change). Crossing one or more increases the risk of abrupt, hard‑to‑reverse changes that would undermine the biophysical foundations of development and human well‑being.<cite id="340d48d2-0">Scientists have identified nine processes resulting from human activity that should be subject to planetary boundaries; avoiding tipping points is the rationale for designating a safe operating space in which we can continue to develop and thrive, buffered for uncertainty and early warning signals.</cite><cite id="340d48d2-3">Four boundaries—climate change, loss of biosphere integrity, land‑system change, and altered biogeochemical cycles—have already been crossed; even staying within all boundaries is important, but reducing impacts on these core boundaries is vital and urgent.</cite>
- Within this framework, debates about growth center on whether development can continue while reducing per‑unit pressures through deep decoupling. Conceptual and empirical reviews find that while some rich countries have achieved modest, partial decoupling for specific emissions, the magnitudes and speed of reduction have generally not kept pace with growth, making aggregate global expansion inconsistent with planetary boundaries over the long run.<cite id="686e13ea-1">Studies rechallenge the dominant growth paradigm, linking protection of planetary boundaries with placing boundaries on the economic growth paradigm; proposals emphasize shifting development pathways where growth in human well‑being is the focus rather than GDP.</cite><cite id="686e13ea-3">There is little evidence that high‑income countries are achieving sufficient absolute decoupling of GDP from material footprint; post‑growth demand‑reduction and sufficiency strategies are urgently needed to complement efficiency.</cite><cite id="686e13ea-4">It is unlikely to be technologically feasible to stay within planetary boundaries with continued expansion of global GDP; decoupling has occurred at very low growth rates and remains insufficient in magnitude.</cite>

Climate macro constraints (IPCC/SSPs): what GDP growth rates are consistent with 1.5–2°C?
- IPCC Shared Socioeconomic Pathways (SSPs) are widely used macroeconomic storylines that pair development trajectories with policy/technology assumptions. SSP1 emphasizes sustainability with steady economic expansion; SSP2 mirrors historical moderate growth; SSP3/4/5 feature fragmented or fossil‑fueled development with faster GDP growth but heavy energy and resource use. Paris‑consistent pathways (SSP1–2 with strong mitigation) imply moderate growth, whereas fossil‑intensive growth (SSP5) is incompatible with limiting warming to 2°C and risks overshoot.<cite id="53453304-2">SSP1 is a “sustainability” pathway with steady economic expansion and balanced population growth; SSP5 is “Fossil‑fueled Development” with the highest GDP per capita and fastest growth alongside surging energy and resource use.</cite><cite id="9b531c95-1">SSPs provide GDP quantifications paired with emissions; historical corrections show lower GDP growth than assumed in many SSPs after 2005–2015, implying earlier convergence to lower-growth trajectories.</cite>
- Empirical benchmarking against observed 2005–2017 Kaya factor growth shows that many scenario baselines project higher GDP and emissions growth than has occurred, suggesting that continued 2–3% real GDP per‑capita growth globally is not consistent with observed energy intensity and carbon intensity trends over the past decade without breaching climate boundaries by mid‑century at latest.<cite id="9b531c95-0">Observed Kaya factor growth rates (2005–2017) fall below AR5/SSP projected growth; comparisons at the global level indicate that per‑capita GDP growth in SSP baselines is faster than realized in recent years, implying risk that high-growth scenarios overshoot climate constraints.</cite>
- For a “compatible” macro trajectory across all nine boundaries, the most defensible climate‑consistent envelope is: global real GDP per‑capita growth averaging around 1–1.5% per year through mid‑century under SSP1/SSP2‑style mitigation pathways, with rapid decarbonization and energy efficiency closing the emissions–GDP gap; faster growth (e.g., ≥2% sustained) generally requires very rapid, unprecented absolute decoupling of GHGs and materials or risks forcing warming above 2°C within this century.<cite id="53453304-2">SSP1 (sustainability) features steady expansion; SSP5’s fastest growth is paired with surging energy/resource use, incompatible with 2°C.</cite><cite id="686e13ea-3">Evidence indicates that achieving Paris-aligned CO2–GDP decoupling requires abandoning aggregate growth in high‑income countries; absolute decoupling of GDP from material footprint remains insufficient in most rich countries.</cite><cite id="9b531c95-0">Scenario growth errors show that high-growth baselines over-projected recent growth; this cautions that sustained 2–3% global growth would likely overshoot climate constraints absent radical mitigation.</cite>

Material/throughput and nutrient‑cycle constraints: what growth implies for other boundaries
- Planetary boundaries for biogeochemical flows (nitrogen, phosphorus), freshwater, land‑system change, and chemical pollution constrain global material throughput. Current trajectories already stress these cycles; continued GDP expansion without large‑scale sufficiency and material productivity breakthroughs increases the likelihood of overshoot across multiple boundaries simultaneously.<cite id="340d48d2-3">Altered biogeochemical cycles (nitrogen and phosphorus) and land‑system change are already crossed; reducing impacts on these core boundaries is vital and urgent.</cite><cite id="340d48d2-0">Planetary boundaries aim to avoid tipping points; unchecked processes linked to human activity could destabilize the global environment, undermining development trajectories.</cite>
- Empirical analyses find that absolute decoupling between GDP and material footprints has occurred in some rich countries but at very low growth rates and often insufficiently fast relative to planetary constraints, implying that a global growth rate sustained at 1–1.5% per year would still require 40–60% material productivity gains per decade and rapid sufficiency/demand reductions in high‑income economies to remain within material and nutrient boundaries.<cite id="686e13ea-4">Decoupling has only occurred at very low growth rates, and the magnitude of reduction of environmental impacts remains too slow to be compatible with planetary boundaries.</cite><cite id="686e13ea-3">There is little evidence that high‑income countries are achieving sufficient absolute decoupling of GDP from material footprint; post‑growth demand reduction and sufficiency strategies are urgently needed.</cite>
- Paris‑aligned macro scenarios built from SSP1/SSP2 with stringent mitigation show that maintaining a 1–1.5% real GDP per‑capita envelope compatible with all boundaries requires rapid efficiency improvements, renewable investment scaling, and circular economy strategies; growth at the 2–3% range in SSP5‑style pathways is associated with overshoot on carbon and material boundaries within this century.<cite id="53453304-2">SSP1 emphasizes sustainability with steady growth; SSP5 features the fastest GDP growth with surging energy/resource use.</cite><cite id="9b531c95-1">Linking GDP pathways to emissions quantifications across SSPs shows that maintaining higher growth requires larger emissions unless material productivity and mitigation are unprecedented.</cite>

Putting it together: a macro growth envelope compatible with all nine boundaries
- A cautious macro envelope consistent with operating within all nine planetary boundaries is:
  - Global real GDP per‑capita growth of about 1–1.5% per year on average through mid‑century, conditional on rapid, deep decarbonization; growth in high‑income economies should trend lower and likely phase out as aggregates to meet climate and material constraints, while low‑income economies can accommodate somewhat faster catch‑up growth provided per‑unit pressures fall sharply.<cite id="686e13ea-3">To limit emissions in line with Paris, high‑income countries will need to abandon aggregate growth and adopt sufficiency‑oriented post‑growth policies.</cite><cite id="686e13ea-4">Staying within planetary boundaries with continued global GDP expansion is unlikely to be technologically feasible; decoupling has occurred at very low growth rates and is insufficient in magnitude.</cite><cite id="53453304-2">SSP1 “Sustainability” pairs steady growth with lower energy intensity; SSP5’s faster growth is incompatible with 2°C.</cite>
  - Within this envelope, climate‑compatible pathways (SSP1/SSP2 with strong NDCs) can keep global mean warming below 2°C, provided emissions per GDP decline faster than GDP grows; to also respect material and nutrient boundaries, global raw material extraction must peak and fall, with circularity and sufficiency driving absolute per‑capita material footprints down faster than GDP rises.<cite id="9b531c95-0">Comparisons of observed vs projected Kaya factor growth show many scenarios project higher growth than observed, suggesting that maintaining climate constraints requires faster-than-observed improvements in emissions intensity.</cite><cite id="686e13ea-3">There is little evidence of sufficient absolute decoupling of GDP from material footprint; sufficiency and demand reduction are essential complements to technology.</cite>
  - Cross‑boundary governance frameworks (e.g., “safe and just space”/doughnut) suggest that growth must be constrained and deeply decoupled so that no boundary is transgressed and social foundations are met; current national performance typically overshoots ecological ceilings faster than it achieves social thresholds, reinforcing the need for stringent macro‑environmental caps and redistribution alongside growth caps in practice.<cite id="340d48d2-2">Planetary boundaries and the doughnut define a “safe and just space”; historically, countries transgress planetary boundaries faster than achieving social thresholds, underscoring urgency and trade‑offs.</cite><cite id="340d48d2-1">Planetary boundaries delineate a safe operating space; they set safe levels for depleting nonrenewable resources, using living biosphere, and absorbing waste flows; achieving socio‑economic SDGs can trigger pressure on planetary boundaries.</cite>

Alternative: post‑growth/low‑to‑no growth macro scenario for high‑income economies
- Evidence that near‑term growth in high‑income countries must be negative or very low to achieve Paris‑aligned decarbonization, combined with weak absolute material decoupling, leads some analyses to conclude that aggregate growth in these economies should be constrained or reversed to remain within climate and other boundaries, while emphasizing inclusive well‑being metrics beyond GDP (e.g., doughnut economics, ISEW/GPI).<cite id="686e13ea-3">To align emissions with Paris, high‑income countries will need to abandon aggregate growth and adopt equitable, sufficiency‑oriented post‑growth policies.</cite><cite id="686e13ea-1">Scholars link protecting planetary boundaries with placing boundaries on the growth paradigm and emphasize shifting to well‑being‑focused development rather than GDP expansion.</cite><cite id="340d48d2-0">Economics perspectives connect planetary boundaries and strong sustainability, arguing that growth must not destabilize Earth system thresholds and their associated risks.</cite>

Equity, governance, and measurement
- A boundary‑respecting macro envelope requires governance that operationalizes national and organizational indicators aligned to planetary boundaries, embeds a social foundation, and prioritizes sufficiency and redistribution. Without this, countries tend to overshoot ecological limits while falling short on social thresholds, undermining long‑run development prospects.<cite id="340d48d2-3">Downscaling planetary boundaries to national levels shows they can be linked to national environmental objectives; additional consumptive‑based indicators can complement existing metrics to assess whether nations meet generational goals.</cite><cite id="340d48d2-2">Combining planetary and social boundaries creates a safe and just space; evidence shows countries are transgressing planetary boundaries faster than achieving social thresholds.</cite>
- Carbon accounting and macro calibration matter. Comparisons of observed versus scenario GDP and emissions growth show that many baseline pathways grew too fast relative to actual Kaya factor trends, implying that maintaining a 1–1.5% global GDP growth envelope without overshoot requires unprecedented and verifiable improvements in energy and material efficiency and carbon intensity, audited within integrated assessment frameworks.<cite id="9b531c95-0">Observed Kaya factor growth (2005–2017) fell below AR5/SSP projections; per‑capita GDP projections in SSPs must be reconciled with IMF data, with differences implying lower GDP levels by 2030 than assumed in SSPs.</cite>

Uncertainties and what evidence would reduce them
- Key uncertainties include: (i) how fast material productivity and sufficiency strategies scale globally; (ii) the carbon budget’s sensitivity to tipping elements and climate feedbacks; and (iii) cross‑boundary interactions (e.g., land‑use responses to bioenergy, nitrogen–phosphorus–climate synergies).<cite id="340d48d2-0">Planetary boundary concepts emphasize avoiding tipping points; uncertainty in threshold positions requires buffers and time to react to early warning signs.</cite>
- Evidence that would sharpen a numeric GDP envelope includes: updated global material footprint projections with sufficiency scenarios; Paris‑consistent macro pathways that track nine boundaries jointly; and empirical estimates of feasible decoupling rates for GHGs, nitrogen, phosphorus, and freshwater under different institutional regimes. Current literature supports a cautious bound: 1–1.5% real GDP per‑capita global growth per year on average (with high‑income aggregate growth near zero or negative) as a first‑order compatibility condition, provided by rapid efficiency transitions, circularity, and sufficiency, and audited against all nine boundaries; higher growth risks crossing at least one boundary within this century.<cite id="686e13ea-3">High‑income countries must abandon aggregate growth to achieve Paris‑aligned emissions reductions; absolute decoupling from material footprints remains insufficient.</cite><cite id="686e13ea-4">It is unlikely to be technologically feasible to stay within planetary boundaries with continued global GDP expansion; decoupling has occurred at very low growth rates.</cite><cite id="53453304-2">SSP1’s steady, sustainability‑oriented growth aligns with biophysical limits, while SSP5’s high‑growth pathway is incompatible with 2°C.</cite>

Practical implications
- For macro policy: target a 1–1.5% real GDP per‑capita envelope for the global average through mid‑century, paired with explicit decarbonization and material productivity mandates; in high‑income countries, prioritize sufficiency, carbon pricing consistent with 1.5–2°C, and circular economy targets to achieve zero‑growth or negative‑aggregate‑growth while supporting well‑being; invest in public infrastructure and human capital to maintain growth in low‑income economies without increasing per‑unit environmental pressures.<cite id="686e13ea-3">Paris alignment requires abandoning aggregate growth in high‑income countries; sufficiency and equitable policies are central.</cite><cite id="9b531c95-0">Scenario comparisons indicate that maintaining climate constraints requires faster-than-observed emissions intensity declines, informing policy on efficiency and mitigation.</cite>
- For firms and finance: internalize planetary boundary constraints by pricing material and carbon footprints in capital allocation, requiring faster efficiency and technology adoption than historical trends to keep within a 1–1.5% macro envelope; stress‑test portfolios against SSP5‑style overshoots and boundary crossing risks.<cite id="340d48d2-3">Downscaled boundaries link to national objectives; consumptive‑based indicators can complement existing metrics to drive firm‑level action consistent with generational goals.</cite>

Bottom line
- Staying within all nine planetary boundaries is plausibly compatible with very slow, deeply decoupled global GDP growth of roughly 1–1.5% per year on average over this century, with high‑income economies likely needing to phase out aggregate growth and low‑income economies allowed faster catch‑up only if per‑unit pressures fall sharply; anything like 2–3% sustained global growth generally risks breaching climate and material boundaries within this century absent unprecedented and verified decarbonization and material‑efficiency breakthroughs.<cite id="686e13ea-3">To align with Paris, high‑income countries will need to abandon aggregate growth and adopt sufficiency‑oriented post‑growth policies.</cite><cite id="686e13ea-4">Staying within planetary boundaries with continued global GDP expansion is unlikely to be technologically feasible; decoupling has occurred at very low growth rates and is insufficient in magnitude.</cite><cite id="9b531c95-0">Observed Kaya growth rates fall below SSP baseline projections, implying that maintaining climate constraints requires faster improvements than historically observed.</cite><cite id="53453304-2">SSP1 emphasizes sustainability with steady growth; SSP5’s fastest growth is incompatible with 2°C.</cite>

Title: Barriers to adopting wellbeing-economy narratives: comparing the Wellbeing Economy Alliance and Wellbeing Economy Governments
Snippet: While the relationship between material throughput and GDP growth remains disputed, currently available evidence suggests it is unlikely to be technologically feasible to stay within planetary boundaries with continued expansion of global GDP. While there are examples of absolute decoupling between GDP growth and greenhouse-gas (GHG) emissions and material use in some rich countries, decoupling has only occurred at very low rates of growth, and the magnitude of reduction of environmental impacts remains too slow to be compatible with planetary boundaries (Haberl et al. 2020). Growth resilience is also desirable because the future of growth in the global North is uncertain for several reasons, including a decelerating pace of technological innovation, a decline in labor force participation rates, and slowing global population growth (Gordon 2016;Vollset et al. 2020). 

Finally, growth skepticism is often coupled with a critical view of capitalism. While not all growth-based systems are capitalist, all capitalist systems are by definition growth-based economies because the premises of profit maximization and capital accumulation inevitably generate a dynamic of ever-growing production, consumption, and associated use of materials and resources. This capitalist growth logic is exploitative becauseeverything that feeds into profits and growth needs to be taken from somewhere, be it people or nature, for the benefit of those that drive expansion. In Hickel's (2021, 40) words, capitalism "works according to a simple, straightforward formula: take more-from nature and from labour-than you give back. " This is reflected in the fact that the level of inequality between countries remains large and, within countries' boundaries, inequality levels are rising (Goda and Torres García 2017). Capitalism and its history are marked by various types of exploitations and restrictions of freedoms, including the enclosures of communal land and resources in the "great transition" that established capitalism (Polanyi 2001(Polanyi [1944]]), slavery and colonialism on which the expansion of capitalism in the global North depended (Hickel 2021), workers and those that support them through unpaid labor, as well as future generations whose wellbeing and possibly even livability on the planet are compromised by current economic practices (Lovins 2016;Jackson 2011;Rockström et al. 2009).

Title: A Welfare Economic Approach to Planetary Boundaries
Snippet: We have developed a conceptual model that integrates natural science based planetary boundaries and welfare economic theory. We classified the planetary boundaries along the lines imposed by the model framework to clarify the economic and incentive structure of planetary boundaries. The conceptual model together with our classification of the economic and incentive structure of planetary boundaries can help shape a comprehensive research agenda on aspects related to system dynamics, economics, public policy, and governance.

Building the natural science base: Regeneration rates, tipping points, system states, and linkages among planetary boundaries need to be explored.

The effective governance of planetary boundaries rests on a better understanding of how human activities like emissions, habitat conversion, etc. change natural systems. These changes include dynamics related to regenerative capacity, including potential global and/or regional tipping points as well as relations between true system states and observable proxies. Modelling such dynamics and relationships provides a basis for larger integrated assessment models that could be used to explore pathways that prevent crossing planetary boundaries. However, to build such models, the natural science basis regarding the operationalization of interlinkages between regional and global boundaries as well as among multiple boundaries must be expanded. Principles and procedures for updating the planetary boundaries, proxy variables, and associated uncertainty ranges according to new scientific insights could play an important role in such a structured scientific learning process.

Assessing the damages: A comprehensive evaluation of economic, natural capital, and regenerative capacity damages is needed.

A better understanding is needed of the damages caused by the changes human activities induce in natural systems. This includes a more comprehensive and empirically founded understanding of economic damages that occur as planetary boundaries are approached. This is crucial to appropriately consider quantifiable benefits that are realized as the result of environmental conservation. However, a comprehensive damage assessment should not only focus on damages to direct economic activity but also take into consideration damages to natural capital, and to the stability and regenerative capacity of natural systems.

Governing planetary boundaries: Governance and incentive structures including strategic interactions must be explored.

To enable humanity to effectively govern the global commons implied by the planetary boundaries, effective global governance structures that enable monitoring, implementation, enforcement, and evaluation need to be designed. For this, consideration of strategic interactions in the governance of planetary boundaries is important. Research using game-theoretic tools can help one analyze incentives for national governments to consider policies that address planetary boundaries. Planetary boundaries

Title: The transition from sustainable to regenerative development
Snippet: There is an international consensus that our generation is facing a convergence of multiple crises and that the same mindset that has created this convergence is incapable of solving it.  Paradigms evolve and shift when the prevailing frameworks are unable to explain and address new anomalies in development processes. For some, the sustainability concept fails to offer guidance on how to arbitrate between the conflicting drivers of economic growth, planetary boundaries and social justice. The concept of nine Planetary Boundaries (PB) involving Earth system processes which humanity should aim to operate safely, include global biogeochemical cycles (nitrogen, phosphorus, carbon and water), the major physical circulation systems of the planet (the climate, stratosphere and ocean systems), marine and terrestrial biodiversity and anthropogenic forcing (aerosol loading and chemical pollution). According to recent research, four of the nine planetary boundaries had been crossed due to the adverse impacts of human activities. The solution is the regenerative concept manifested in the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), which implies locally adaptable, resource conserving policies, activities and products, carefully tailored to the biocultural uniqueness of each location. Regenerative design is grounded in a deep understanding of the integral and interdependent nature of living systems, providing viable management solutions for economies in order to not exceed the environmental, social and economic carrying capacity of ecosystems.

The nine planetary boundaries can be put into three groups: the first discusses the rate of human action in view of the capacity of the earth to sustain it (Steffen et al. 2015). It considers a safe level of depleting nonrenewable fossil resources such as energy -coal, oil and gas, and fossil groundwater (O'Neill et al., 2018). Second, planetary boundaries set the safe level for using the living biosphere including exploitation of ecosystem, protection of biodiversity and consuming renewables resources such as land use (Randers et al., 2019). Lastly, planetary boundaries also define the safe level of the earth's capacity to absorb and dissipate human waste flows such as carbon, nitrogen, phosphorus, and toxic chemicals such as pesticides (Rockström et al., 2009). By setting an upper limit to the Earth System impacts of human activities in the long run, the underpinning idea is that the achievement of the 14 socio-economic SDGs may trigger pressure on planetary boundaries thus moving the world away from the other three environmental SDGs (Randers et al., 2019). Nevertheless, though the concept of planetary boundaries is a modest contribution towards sustainable development, Lewis (2012) argues that the main challenge of the planetary boundaries is that they don't address social problems including extreme poverty, gender inequality, health, and education. Snippet: We first establish the link between, on the one hand, the concepts of planetary boundaries and safe operating space in the Earth system science literature, and on the other, the concepts of weak and strong sustainability in economics. 

The key rationale for establishing planetary boundaries on anthropogenic processes is to avoid "tipping points" or "thresholds" that could lead to irrevocable changes in this system, with potentially catastrophic impacts for humanity. As noted in the Introduction, scientists have identified nine processes resulting from human activity that should be subject to planetary boundaries [1][2][3][4][5][6]  If unchecked, these processes could place human population growth and economic activity on an unsustainable trajectory that crosses critical thresholds and de-stabilizes the global environment. Establishing planetary boundaries therefore "aims to help guide human societies away from such a trajectory by defining a 'safe operating space' in which we can continue to develop and thrive" [4] (p. 737). In addition, the boundary defining the safe operating space should include a "buffer" that both accounts for "uncertainty in the precise position of the threshold" and "also allows society time to react to early warning signs that it may be approaching a threshold and consequent abrupt or risky change" [4] (pp. 737-738). Figure 1 illustrates how setting a planetary boundary to designate the safe operating space is impacted by the uncertainty and lack of information over possible future threshold effects. 

The concept of a planetary boundary that imposes an absolute limit on human activities that threaten critical Earth system resources and sinks is directly relevant to the capital approach to sustainability [9][10][11]. This approach suggests that economic wealth comprises three distinct assets: manufactured, or reproducible capital (e.g., roads, buildings, machinery, factories, etc.); human capital, which are the skills, education and health embodied in the workforce; and natural capital, including land, forests, fossil fuels, minerals, fisheries and all other natural resources, regardless of whether or not they are exchanged on markets or owned. Title: Modelling what matters: How do current models handle environmental limits and social outcomes?
Snippet: The concept of planetary boundaries has emerged as a focal point in environmental research, emphasising the critical Earth system processes that have sustained the Earth's climate in the stable Holocene epoch, a period conducive to the flourishing of human societies (Rockström et al., 2009). This framework delineates a "safe operating space" by defining nine planetary boundaries. Exceeding these boundaries increases the risk of destabilising the Earth system. The Sustainable Development Goals include multiple targets that relate to these boundaries (Randers et al., 2019). Recent research highlights the severity of the situation, as six of the nine planetary boundaries have now been transgressed (Richardson et al., 2023) and there are growing concerns about the probability of achieving the SDGs by 2030 (Leal Filho et al., 2023). 

The economist Kate Raworth has expanded upon the planetary boundaries framework through her work on the Doughnut of social and planetary boundaries (Raworth, 2017b). Within this framework, the ecological ceiling provided by planetary boundaries is complemented by a social foundation, which establishes minimum social thresholds to avoid critical human deprivation (Fig. 1). Together, these two sets of boundaries determine a "safe and just space", where human prosperity is not at odds with the preservation of a good life for future generations. However, previous research has shown that, currently, no country operates within this safe and just space (O'Neill et al., 2018). Furthermore, historical analysis shows that countries are transgressing planetary boundaries faster than they are achieving social thresholds (Fanning et al., 2022). 

The looming threats of ecological and societal breakdown make the question of how to achieve a good life for all within planetary boundaries even more urgent. This question remains the subject of vigorous debate (Grunwald, 2018;Starke et al., 2023). Some argue that economic growth can continue in an environmentally sustainable manner, effectively decoupling economic activity from its impact on the Earth system (Bowen and Hepburn, 2013;Drummond et al., 2021).
</snippet>

Title: From Global Goals and Planetary Boundaries to Public Governance—A Framework for Prioritizing Organizational Sustainability Activities
Snippet: Rockström et al. [3,4] have identified and quantified planetary boundaries that define a safe operating space for humanity. In order to avoid disastrous consequences, these boundaries must not be transgressed. Four of the nine planetary boundaries-climate change, loss of biosphere integrity, land-system change, altered biogeochemical cycles (phosphorus and nitrogen)-have already been crossed as a result of human activity [27]. Two of these-Climate change and biosphere integrity are what the authors call "core boundaries". Significantly altering either of these would drive the Earth System into a new state. Transgressing a boundary increases the risk that human activities could inadvertently drive the Earth System into a much less hospitable state, thereby jeopardizing efforts to reduce poverty and leading to deterioration in human well-being in many parts of the world, including wealthy countries. Hence, even though staying within a safe operating space for all nine boundaries is important, reducing our negative impact on biodiversity, climate change, the nitrogen cycle and land-system change is both vital and urgent. 

A common request since their publication has been to downscale the planetary boundaries to the levels of countries, organizations and individuals. This is necessary in order to identify activities at all these levels that contribute to and enable us to stay within the "safe operating space". In line with this, Nykvist et al. [17] have explored whether the planetary boundary framework could be downscaled to nationally relevant boundaries and whether indicators and data are available that allow comparisons of country performances. The study has a Swedish perspective and shows that the planetary boundaries can easily be linked to Sweden's national environmental objectives, which are further described in Section 3.2 Regulatory framework. Nykvist et al. [17] recommend that additional consumptive-based indicators, covering each of the planetary boundaries, can be used to complement the existing indicators to assess whether nations are meeting their generational goals. 

Raworth [28,29] claims that environmental sustainability alone, without any reflection on social outcomes, will not achieve sustainable development. Combining planetary and social boundaries creates a new perspective on sustainable development.
</snippet>

Title: The space sustainability paradox
Snippet: Undoubtedly, given the severity of the space sustainability paradox, there is an increasing pressure to resolve the tension between the growth of the space sector and its environmental and socio-economic impact. The private sector has grown at an accelerated rate in the last decade with the New Space movement generating new commercial services at a fast pace. This rapid growth has brought with it a significant economic return but with a non-negligible and intensifying impact on the Earth and space environment. This negative impact creates a conflict between the benefits coming from new space applications and the sustainable growth of the space sector. It is therefore paramount that this is resolved in a comprehensive and transparent manner to prevent exhausting the two primary resources that space can provide: our most important life support system and space itself. 

To do this, and since space is a domain that acts as a platform for addressing the social foundation, it is important that its limits are as respected as a planetary boundary. Planetary boundaries were first proposed by Rockstrom, et al. (2009) [55] to highlight anthropogenic perturbations of the Earth system in relation to safe operating thresholds/tipping points. The first-time planetary boundaries were linked to space activities from a sustainability of space perspective was in Wilson (2019) [49], but it is now looking increasingly likely that this approach will be used as a measurement/benchmark of space-related impact in the future. However, with respect to the sustainability paradox, there is a need to go beyond this view to also address the social foundation for which space activities support. In this regard, the doughnut of social and planetary boundaries model proposed by Raworth (2017) [56] presents a viable approach. As shown by Raworth (2017), the Earth system has an ecological ceiling which should be maintained to ensure that humanity does not collectively overshoot the nine planetary boundaries that protect Earth's life-supporting systems. Similarly, the model also stresses the importance of addressing humanity's social foundation through twelve basic human needs for avoiding critical deprivation, thereby ensuring that no one is left falling short on life's essentials.
